I've always been an advocate of Bleep. Runs on the BitTorrent distribution network. The only thing better than your own server is an absence of servers. The conversation is as secure as the people having it, which, in this day and age, isn't saying much. But it says more than any other messaging platform I've used.

Of course, there's basically no refuge from surveillance in this day and age. Keystrokes, screenshots, browser traffic, all of these can be recorded surreptitiously and in an automated fashion. Siri and Google Now have demonstrated that our microphones can listen, always on, for specific words that'll initiate a recording. Who's to say the only words it knows are "Okay, Google?" Perhaps our devices are waiting for us to say "assassination," "infidels," etc.

The same goes for messaging, and I'll again point out a Google feature. Now on Tap (which I think has a new name, but that's what it launched as,) can read any words on your screen and suggest relevant content. Ask a friend if they want to get dinner, it'll show you restaurants nearby. In fact, my phone's keyboard just suggested I search "restaurants near me" after I typed that. The potential of stuff like this is pretty horrifying.

The only reason I'm not afraid to use Google products is because I know when to trust them, when to use an air gapped Pine64 for programming, and when to just write shit down. Our new President doesn't even use email, opting to instead send important info via courier. The CEO of Facebook, the Director of the FBI, and the Pope all cover their webcams. In fact, Zuckerberg also has tape over his headphone jack, which I have suspicions about.

Surveillance isn't impressive. What's impressive is the scale it's taken.
